planHeader: This remediation plan is advisory text generated from read-only scan findings.
This tool changed nothing on your machine and will not run any of these steps.
Read every step before running it. You are the operator; commands run by you.
If sequence-sensitive persistence is present, follow the STOP guidance before any credential rotation; rotate only later from a separate clean device.
If you are unsure at any point, stop and get incident-response help before continuing.
deadManBanner: STOP - READ THIS BEFORE TOUCHING ANYTHING
One or more findings match persistence that is reported to include a
DEAD-MAN'S SWITCH. If you remove files or revoke credentials in the wrong
order, the switch can fire and damage this machine.
NOTIFY ONLY / READ-ONLY GUIDANCE: Do not blindly delete, disable, or remove
any files, services, or tokens until further guidance from security teams.
Preserve evidence. Coordinate ordered response with incident responders.
When security authorizes action, follow STOP items below in exact order
before other cleanup and before rotating any tokens.

rules.title: GitHub token dead-man's switch (gh-token-monitor persistence)

evidence.status: historical-confirmed capability; local installation or activation must be established
evidence.confidence: high for documented behavior, not for current activity on this host

warning: Independent incident research documented this persistence watching a GitHub token and reacting when it is revoked; a match does not establish that the infrastructure or campaign is currently active.

August analyses differed on activation: some observed or reconstructed operational behavior, while another found the capability embedded without an observed call site. Confirm local installation and service state before classifying it as armed.
NOTIFY ONLY: Do not blindly delete or remove anything until further guidance from security teams.
Do NOT revoke or rotate GitHub tokens from a possibly infected host.
Do NOT delete monitor files while any related service may still be running, unless security directs you.

Related incident research documents production-crash extortion language if a stolen API key is blocked; still treat dead-man findings as notify-only until incident response directs ordered disarm and then rotation.
steps: Notify security / incident response and preserve evidence (paths, unit status, timestamps). Do not run destructive cleanup yet.
When security authorizes ordered response, Linux: systemctl --user stop gh-token-monitor.service
When security authorizes: systemctl --user disable gh-token-monitor.service
When security authorizes: remove ~/.config/systemd/user/gh-token-monitor.service (after stop)
When security authorizes: remove ~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh and ~/.config/gh-token-monitor/
When security authorizes: macOS unload/remove com.user.gh-token-monitor.plist and related paths
When security authorizes and monitor is confirmed stopped: rotate GitHub tokens from a separate clean device
Rebuild or reimage high-value CI runners if install-time execution is confirmed
doNotDo: Do not blindly delete files, services, or tokens without security-team guidance.
Do not revoke GitHub tokens before the monitor is confirmed stopped under IR direction.
Do not run cleanup from another account or host that shares these tokens until rotation is done from a clean machine.

rules.title: August 2026 keyv/ChainDrop operator actions

evidence.status: historical campaign reporting; per-host dead-man presence requires separate evidence
evidence.confidence: high for corroborated exact package/version artifacts; current activity and per-host persistence require separate evidence

warning: Independent incident inventories disagree on their dated totals; this scanner includes 2,236 exact package/version pairs across 444 packages corroborated by at least two inventories retrieved 2026-08-12.
Package/version, broad text, namespace, infrastructure, and editor-hook matches do not prove an installed or armed dead-man switch.
The production-crash extortion string and campaign encryption key are historical incident signals; neither is a dead-man trigger by itself.
This tool remains read-only. Only exact local gh-token-monitor persistence artifacts are eligible for sequence-sensitive STOP guidance.
steps: Preserve evidence (lockfiles, package metadata, unit status, IDE config hooks) without deleting yet.
If gh-token-monitor or other dead-man persistence is present, follow STOP-deadman rules first under IR direction before any token revoke.
From a separate clean device: rotate keys and enable 2FA on source control, package registries, cloud, SSH, and related accounts.
Downgrade affected packages to known-safe versions; reinstall only after checking the scanner's dated corroborated inventory and current independent advisories.

Search for affected source-control accounts and repositories (including 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again' description markers) and revoke/remove them only after any confirmed sequence-sensitive persistence is safely handled.
Re-scan the tree with this read-only scanner after containment work completes.
doNotDo: Do not blindly delete files, services, or tokens without security-team guidance.
Do not revoke GitHub tokens while dead-man monitor persistence may still be armed, unless IR directs the order.
Do not treat package presence alone as evidence that a dead-man monitor is installed, active, or armed.

rules.title: Historical PyPI monitor persistence (pgsql-monitor / pgmonitor)

evidence.status: historical persistence; dead-man behavior and current activity unverified

warning: The reported PyPI payload installed monitor-style persistence. Available evidence does not establish this entry as an active dead-man switch.
Treat a match as sequence-sensitive persistence review: contact incident response before changing the service, files, or credentials.
steps: Follow docs/recovery-playbook.md with incident response; this scanner performs no removal.
Have incident response verify whether the service exists, what it launches, and whether it is active before authorizing changes.
If removal is authorized, stop/disable persistence before removing its unit or payload files.
Only after persistence is safely handled should exposed credentials be rotated from a separate clean device.
doNotDo: Do not classify pgmonitor/pgsql-monitor as an active dead-man switch from the name alone.
Do not rotate credentials or delete evidence before incident response determines the safe order.

rules.title: Monitor-style persistence (kitty-monitor / cat.py)

evidence.status: historical persistence; dead-man behavior and current activity unverified

warning: This is a historical monitor-style persistence indicator. The evidence does not establish kitty-monitor as a dead-man switch.
A generic cat.py basename does not trigger this rule; require the specific service/plist artifact and review context.
steps: Follow docs/recovery-playbook.md with incident response; this scanner performs no removal.
Have incident response verify the service/plist target and active state before authorizing changes.
If removal is authorized, unload or stop persistence before removing the unit, plist, or referenced payload.
Only after persistence is safely handled should exposed credentials be rotated from a separate clean device.
doNotDo: Do not treat cat.py alone as malware or an active dead-man switch.
Do not rotate credentials or delete files before incident response determines the safe order.

rules.title: AI-agent / editor config persistence (.claude, .vscode, .cursor, .gemini)
warning: This persistence fires when an AI agent or editor opens the folder.
Stop opening this project in AI agents, Cursor, or VS Code until it is cleaned.
steps: Close any AI-agent or editor session that has this folder open
From a clean environment, review .claude/settings*.json hooks, .vscode/tasks.json, .cursor/rules/*.mdc, and .gemini settings in this project
Remove hook, task, or rule entries that run node .github/setup.js, payload filenames, or other unexpected commands
Review .github/setup.js itself as a reported reinfection payload path before any CI or package scripts run
Re-scan after cleaning to confirm the trigger entries are gone
doNotDo: Do not assume npm uninstall or pip uninstall removed persistence from tool config files.
Do not open this folder in an AI agent or editor with automation enabled until the config is clean.

rules.title: easy-day-js / Mastra stage-2 persistence (protocal.cjs / NodePackages)
warning: Socket reports this Mastra/easy-day-js stage-2 as cross-platform persistence and browser/wallet/credential collection.
Stop or unload persistence before deleting files, and preserve evidence before any cleanup.
This is ordered manual incident guidance, not a dead-man's-switch rule.
steps: Stop package installs, builds, dev servers, and Node processes tied to the affected project
Review lockfiles, install logs, suspicious NodePackages directories, .pkg_history, .pkg_logs, and browser-hist-* artifacts before deletion
Windows: remove the NvmProtocal Run-key entry only after exporting the key and preserving C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\protocal.cjs plus config.json metadata
macOS: launchctl unload ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.nvm.protocal.plist if present, then preserve and remove the plist and ~/Library/NodePackages/protocal.cjs
Linux: systemctl --user stop nvmconf.service, then systemctl --user disable nvmconf.service if present
Linux: preserve and remove the nvmconf systemd user unit, ~/.config/systemd/nvmconf/protocal.cjs, and ~/.config/NodePackages/config.json
Verify no protocal.cjs, NvmProtocal, com.nvm.protocal, nvmconf.service, NodePackages, .pkg_history, .pkg_logs, or browser-hist-* artifacts remain in user and project paths
After persistence and payload artifacts are handled, rotate npm, GitHub, cloud, SSH, browser-stored, wallet, and CI credentials from a separate clean device
Rebuild the dependency tree from a clean environment with install scripts blocked and known-bad Mastra/easy-day-js versions pinned away
doNotDo: Do not delete protocal.cjs or NodePackages artifacts before preserving evidence.
Do not rotate credentials from the suspected infected host.
Do not run a normal npm install while known-bad versions remain in the manifest or lockfile.

rules.title: procwire / routecraft Windows npm dropper
warning: SafeDep reports this npm campaign as a Windows-only install-time binary dropper.
If the affected package was installed on Windows, treat the host as compromised until triaged.
Preserve evidence before deleting dropped executables or rebuilding dependency state.
steps: Stop npm installs, builds, tests, dev servers, and editor tasks in the affected project
Review package.json, lockfiles, npm logs, and node_modules evidence before cleanup
On Windows, inspect %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp, %TEMP%, and %TMP% for recent msedge_update_*.exe, chrome_installer_*.exe, dotnet_host_*.exe, onedrive_setup_*.exe, or teams_update_*.exe files
Preserve file paths, hashes, timestamps, Zone.Identifier alternate data stream state, and process/network evidence before removal
Check for outbound access to files.catbox.moe, especially /j4loim.chk and the Microsoft-Delivery-Optimization/10.0 user-agent
Remove known-bad procwire, routecraft, endpointmap, bytecraft, and staticlayer versions from manifests and lockfiles
Regenerate dependency state from a clean environment with install scripts blocked
Rotate npm, GitHub, cloud, SSH, browser-stored, and CI credentials from a separate clean device if execution may have occurred
doNotDo: Do not run npm install again in the affected tree until known-bad package versions are removed.
Do not delete updater-named executables before preserving metadata and hashes.
Do not rotate credentials from the suspected infected Windows host.

rules.title: BLUERABBIT Windows backdoor / ransomware indicators
warning: Binary Defense reports BLUERABBIT as a Windows Golang backdoor with exfiltration, ransomware, and destructive disk-wiping capabilities.
If these indicators are found on a Windows host, treat the system as potentially compromised and destructive until triaged.
Preserve evidence before changing scheduled tasks, registry keys, encrypted files, or recovery settings.
steps: Stop normal user activity, installs, builds, and automation on the affected Windows host
If execution is suspected, isolate the host from the network while preserving volatile evidence where incident-response policy allows
Review scheduled-task, registry, process, service, network, and file-system evidence before cleanup
Review the scheduled task named OneDrive Update, especially tasks created with hidden/immediate/startup behavior or AllowStartIfOnBatteries
Review HKCU\Software\OneDrive\Environment and recovery-suppression registry values such as AutoReboot, NoAutoRebootWithLoggedOnUsers, MaintenanceDisabled, and AlwaysAutoRebootAtScheduledTime
Search for .candy encrypted files, High-Alert wallpaper changes, GUID-named staging directories, and evidence of RabbitMQ/AMQP, Redis, or S3-compatible MinIO exfiltration
Check file hashes against the reported SHA-256 indicators before deleting or rebuilding

Rotate credentials from a separate clean device after containment and evidence capture; prioritize domain, VPN, cloud, GitHub, package-registry, SSH, browser-stored, banking, and crypto credentials exposed from that host
Prefer rebuild/reimage from a clean baseline if payload execution, encryption, wiping, or credential access is confirmed
doNotDo: Do not remove the scheduled task, registry keys, or suspected payload before preserving evidence.
Do not rotate credentials from the suspected infected Windows host.
Do not assume disabling encryption stops wiping or backdoor capability.

rules.title: Known payload files or second-stage code on disk
warning: Payload files on disk mean execution may already have happened.
Order matters: isolate and preserve evidence BEFORE deleting anything.
steps: Stop package installs, builds, test runners, and dev servers in this project
If payload execution is possible, disconnect this host from the network
Review lockfiles, package manifests, and install logs before cleanup
Preserve the flagged files' metadata (path, size, timestamps, hash) before removal
Check ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and known_hosts if SSH-propagation findings are present, and triage downstream hosts this machine can reach
If any dead-man's-switch items appear above, complete them before removing payload files
Treat confirmed execution or credential access as host compromise: rebuild or reimage from a clean baseline
Rotate GitHub, npm, cloud, Vault, Kubernetes, SSH, and CI secrets from a separate clean device
doNotDo: Do not run cleanup commands from the suspected infected environment.
Do not delete payload files before preserving evidence.
Do not rely on the absence of obvious damage as proof the payload did not run.

rules.title: Compromised package versions in manifests or lockfiles
steps: Stop installs and builds in this project until dependency state is corrected
Determine whether the compromised version was actually installed (check node_modules, site-packages, vendor/, and install logs) - referenced-but-never-installed is a much smaller blast radius
Pin away from every flagged version in the manifest
Delete the resolved dependency tree (node_modules / vendor / venv) rather than trusting partial cleanup
Regenerate the lockfile from a clean environment with install scripts blocked (npm ci --ignore-scripts or equivalent)
If the compromised version was installed and its scripts ran, switch to the payload-on-disk steps above and treat this as possible host compromise
doNotDo: Do not run a plain install to 'fix' versions while known-bad packages are still referenced.
Do not keep the old lockfile after pinning away - regenerate it.

rules.title: CI workflow exposure (GitHub Actions / Claude Code Action)
steps: Review the flagged workflow files and disable any you did not author or cannot explain
Audit recent Actions runs for secret exfiltration (encoded output, unexpected network posts)
Audit the repository and org for recently created tokens, suspicious repositories, unexpected workflows, and self-hosted runners
For Claude Code Action: update to v1.0.94 or newer, restrict allowed_non_write_users, and remove write permissions and OIDC (id-token: write) from workflows reachable by untrusted issue/PR input
If a workflow exfiltrated secrets, rotate the exposed secrets from a clean device (after any dead-man's-switch items above)
doNotDo: Do not re-run flagged workflows to 'see what they do'.
Do not leave id-token: write enabled on workflows triggered by untrusted input.

rules.title: Apache mod_http2 below CVE-2026-49975 fix floor
steps: Upgrade mod_http2 to 2.0.41 or newer, or disable HTTP/2 (remove h2 from Protocols) until patched
Verify the running module version matches the config you inspected
This is a patching item, not malware removal - no compromise ordering applies

rules.title: Review items (campaign-adjacent packages, GitHub-sourced deps, lifecycle scripts, tool shadowing)
steps: Verify each flagged package's exact version against the known-bad lists and upstream advisories
Read flagged lifecycle scripts and binding.gyp command expansions before allowing any install to run them
For GitHub-sourced dependency specs, confirm the commit matches the real upstream repository
For tool-shadowing candidates, compare the file against the real tool and remove repo-local fakes from PATH
Prefer installs with scripts blocked (npm ci --ignore-scripts or equivalent) until everything flagged is verified
doNotDo: Do not delete anything in this category before verifying - these are review signals, not confirmed malware.

likely-exposed: Work through the items above in the order printed: STOP items first, then CAUTION, then REVIEW.
This scanner does not save or retain findings; JSON is stdout-only.
After cleanup, re-run this scanner; a clean result means these indicators are gone, not that the host is proven clean.
If payload execution is confirmed, rebuild from a clean baseline rather than trusting spot cleanup.
possible-exposure: Work through the items above before running further installs or builds.
This scanner does not save or retain findings; JSON is stdout-only.
Re-run this scanner after addressing the findings.
review-needed: These findings are review signals, not confirmed compromise.
Verify the flagged items before your next install or build, then re-run this scanner.
no-known-indicators: No known indicators were found, so there is nothing to remediate from this scan.
This does not prove the host is clean; it only covers indicators this tool knows about.
